subject: Post-call: Orion Health streaming SLOs + cost levers — next steps
messages:
From: Alex Kim <alex.kim@orionhealth.com>
To: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 7 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Initial discovery — Orion Health real-time transcription use case

Thanks for the call this morning — helpful conversation. Quick recap from our side and a couple questions so you can size options: 

Summary of our requirements
- Primary flow: live clinical dictation into EHR; physicians expect first-word latency to be low and final transcript to arrive within a short window.
- Expected peak concurrency: ~40 simultaneous doctors during business hours; long tail to 60 for peak events.
- Average response size: 250-700 tokens per record (most around 400 tokens).
- Soft p95 SLO target (final transcript complete): <= 250 ms for local notes, but we can stretch to 350 ms if it meaningfully reduces cost.
- Streaming requirement: yes — incremental partial transcripts acceptable; first-byte target <= 120 ms.
- Throughput target: sustain 80–100 requests/sec during peak; burst to 150 rps for 5–10 minutes.

Questions for Redwood engineering & pricing
1) For the p95 targets above, what are the concrete levers you recommend (continuous batching, prefix caching, model variants, quantization)?
2) What latency/throughput tradeoffs should we expect if we add 4-bit quantization vs int8?
3) For streaming, does your runtime support partial outputs without significant overhead on KV cache/concurrency?
4) Any recommended config to keep cost per completed transcript under $0.02?

Attachments: I attached our raw SLOs worksheet (Orion_SLOs_RawNotes.xlsx).

Next steps:
- We can share sample transcripts if helpful.
- We’d like a short follow-up with suggested config and rough cost ranges this week.

Thanks,
Alex
Alex Kim
Program Manager, Clinical IT
Orion Health

From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.com>
To: Alex Kim <alex.kim@orionhealth.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 7 Apr 2027 10:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: Orion Health streaming SLOs + cost levers — next steps

Alex — thanks for the clear notes and the worksheet. Short answers up front, then proposed next steps and owners.

Top-level recommendations (brief)
- Streaming + first-byte <= 120ms: use a dedicated low-latency pool (Reserved/Dedicated) with a streaming-optimized model variant. Prioritize small-batched real-time sessions instead of large continual batching for first-byte.
- Final p95 <= 250–350ms: achievable with a combination of model variant selection + continuous batching for mid-token segments. Use KV prefix caching for repeated phrases (clinical templates) to shave 30–80ms on average.
- Cost levers: aggressive quantization (int8 for production; experiment with 4-bit for non-critical workloads), model distillation/trimmed head variants, and request-level batching heuristics.

Answers to your questions
1) Concrete levers: continuous batching (set target window ~20ms for streaming-mediated flows), KV/prefix caching for repeated phrases, model variants (base-1024 vs trimmed-512 hidden size) depending on exact token length distribution, and quantization tiering (int8 -> primary; 4-bit for low-latency, lower-accuracy non-critical paths).
2) Quantization tradeoffs: int8 typically preserves >98% of perceived fidelity for clinical dictation; 4-bit can reduce inference cost by ~30–45% but may introduce subtle artifacts — recommend running an eval suite on your prompt set. Latency improves modestly (10–20ms) depending on kernel efficiency.
3) Streaming support: yes — runtime supports partial outputs and maintains KV cache across streaming chunks. Overhead is small if you pin sessions on a dedicated worker; autoscaled shared pools see slightly higher tail latency under high concurrency.
4) Cost target: $0.02/transcript is ambitious for 400-token averages at strict p95; options to approach it: strong prefix caching, using trimmed/quantized variants for non-critical segments, and hybrid routing (hosted for baseline, dedicated for peaks). We’ll model several scenarios in the follow-up doc.

Proposed next steps (owners & timeline)
- Redwood (Marcus): run a quick model/profile matrix (latency vs tokens vs quantization) using sample transcripts. Deliverable: table with estimated p50/p95 latency and cost per transcript by Fri 2027-04-09.
- Redwood (Lauren): draft recommended runtime config (batch window, cache TTL, concurrency settings, streaming flags) and a canary rollout plan for Orion’s Dedicated environment. Deliverable: config doc + short roadmap by Mon 2027-04-12.
- Orion (Alex): share 100 representative transcripts and highlight top 10 repeated templates. Deliverable: sample set by Thu 2027-04-08.

I attached a short primer on quantization profiles we typically share and a mutual action plan draft.

Attachments: Redwood-quantization-profiles.pdf; mutual-action-plan-ORH-2027.docx

Thanks — I’ll kick off the profiling run with Marcus now.

— Sergio
Sergio Alvarez
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
sergio@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0198

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
To: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.com>, Alex Kim <alex.kim@orionhealth.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 8 Apr 2027 09:18:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: Orion Health streaming SLOs + cost levers — next steps

Thanks — I ran a quick sanity profiling pass against a trimmed clinical model variant using a small sample Alex uploaded this morning. High-level results below (rough estimates):

Profiling summary (sample ~80 transcripts, avg 420 tokens)
- Model: redwood-small-rt (trimmed runtime variant)
- Quantization: int8 -> p95 final-transcript latency: ~270ms; p50: ~140ms.
- Quantization: 4-bit -> p95: ~230ms; p50: ~125ms, but error rate (WER-like) increased on stuttered dictation by ~3.5% on our heuristics.
- Continuous batching window 15–25ms (for streaming) reduced CPU/GPU overhead and lowered cost ~12% vs no batching, with negligible impact on first-byte when sessions are pinned to a low-latency pool.
- Prefix caching: for templates we saw average token savings ~18% and p95 improvement ~35–60ms depending on template frequency.
- Concurrency behavior: pinned dedicated workers held p95 under 300ms at 45 concurrent sessions; shared pools saw p95 degradation to ~420ms when concurrency >70.

Preliminary cost estimate (very rough)
- int8 + dedicated pool + caching: $0.028/transcript (avg 420 tokens).
- 4-bit + dedicated pool + caching: $0.019/transcript but with the observed fidelity drop on corner cases.

Notes and recommendations
- If Orion cannot tolerate the 4-bit fidelity delta on PII-heavy or critical notes, we recommend int8 and focusing on caching + model trimming.
- For burst handling, enable autoscale with a fallback to a slightly cheaper model variant to preserve availability.

Next steps I’ll take this afternoon:
- Run the full 100-sample eval with A/B quality checks across int8 vs 4-bit and produce a short table. Target: EOD 2027-04-08.

-Marcus
Marcus Lin
Senior Performance Engineer | Redwood Inference
marcus@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Post-call: Orion Health streaming SLOs + cost levers — next steps

Appreciate the fast turn. This is very helpful and gives us the concrete tradeoffs we needed. Two quick items: 

1) We’ll proceed with the 100-sample set upload by EOD and highlight the 12 clinician templates we rely on most.
2) On the tradeoff table, could you also add an estimated compliance/regulatory note for each quantization tier (e.g., anything that affects de-identification or traceability)? We have to validate with our security & compliance team before trying 4-bit in prod.

If the full eval confirms the 4-bit fidelity drop only on noisy inputs, we may pilot 4-bit for transcription of post-visit follow-ups (lower risk) and int8 for primary clinical notes. 

Let’s plan a short sync next Tue (2027-04-13) to review the tables and a canary plan.

Thanks,
Alex
